title: The back shop
hook: keep a room behind the shop, all your own, where true freedom lives (Essays 1.39)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Montaigne's question: who are the barbarians? Did you catch yourself starting a sentence with those people, and did the question slow it down? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

A parked car in the driveway, engine off, with somebody still sitting in it. The groceries can wait three more minutes. So can the people inside. Or the shower with the fan running, or the long way home from the store. Maybe you have a spot like that, a few minutes nobody else can reach. Montaigne had one too, and a name for it. He didn't take the name from a monastery or a mountain. He took it from a shop.
screen: `A PARKED CAR, ENGINE OFF.` → `THREE MORE MINUTES.` → `A NAME FROM A SHOP.`

segments.voice: First, the room. In his essay Of Solitude, Montaigne says we should set aside a back shop, all our own, entirely free, where we keep our true liberty and our main retreat. Picture a small shop. Out front, the counter, the customers, the bell on the door. Behind a curtain, a back room. That's where the shopkeeper sits down. In the back shop, he says, we hold our ordinary talk with ourselves, so privately that nothing from outside gets in. Second, the people out front. This isn't a plan to run away. He says to have a spouse, children, goods, and above all health, if we can. Just don't be so tied to them that our happiness hangs on them. Love the front of the shop. Don't live only there. Third, the trip you can't take. Leaving the crowd, he says, isn't enough on its own. We carry our worries and wants with us, even into the quietest place. Moving to the country doesn't empty the mind. The retreat has to happen inside, or it doesn't happen. Fourth, belonging to yourself. In the same essay he writes that the greatest thing in the world is knowing how to belong to yourself. Not to your job, not to your reputation, not even to the people you love most, at least not all the way down. Last week we met his tower. The tower was a building. The back shop is portable. On an ordinary Tuesday, it can be ten minutes, a closed door, and nothing to produce.
screen: `A ROOM BEHIND THE SHOP.` · `LOVE THE FRONT, DON'T LIVE THERE.` · `YOU CAN'T OUTRUN YOUR WORRIES.` · `BELONG TO YOURSELF.` · then, large: `THE BACK SHOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: open the back shop. Sit, and let the front of the shop go quiet. The phone face down, the list put away. Notice the voices that usually follow you in: a request, a worry, somebody's opinion of you. Let each one wait at the counter. Behind the curtain there's a small room where nobody needs anything from you. Sit in it and breathe. Later today, find ten minutes like this, all your own, and guard them. The bell holds the time.
The back shop. Montaigne's room behind the counter, all our own, where we keep our freedom and talk with ourselves. Today's word.
Your line: the back shop. Today, keep ten minutes that belong to nobody else. If someone knocks, the front of the shop is still open. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often take the back shop as a daily habit: a short, protected stretch of time, kept free even in a full life of family and work.

myth: Montaigne tells readers to give up family and goods for solitude
he says to have them if we can, just not to let our happiness hang on them.
he says going somewhere quiet isn't enough on its own
we carry our worries with us; the retreat has to happen inside.
the back shop is a place for talking with yourself
he says we hold our ordinary talk with ourselves there, so privately nothing from outside gets in.

fork.setup: you have a family, a job and a house, and you want what Montaigne calls true liberty. what does he advise?
options: leave it all for a life apart.
keep them, and keep a back room in yourself that doesn't depend on them.
work harder now so you can be free later.
fork.reveal: he says to have spouse, children and goods if we can, but to set aside a back shop, all our own, where our freedom lives.

original.note: French, Montaigne's word in Of Solitude: the back shop, the room behind the counter.

trapdoor: what you thought: the back shop is about getting away from people.
what it means: it's an inner room you keep while living fully among others, so your happiness doesn't hang on any one thing.
what a scholar hears: the image comes from the marketplace, not the monastery. the shop stays open; there's just a room behind it.

sources.ref: Essays 1.39, Of Solitude (reserve a back shop all our own, entirely free; have spouse, children, goods and health if we can, but not so bound that our happiness depends on them; leaving the crowd is not enough; the greatest thing is to know how to belong to oneself)

notes: All Montaigne is paraphrased (Cotton/Hazlitt not on the validator's public-domain list).
'The greatest thing in the world is to know how to belong to oneself' is paraphrased from 1.39 (la plus grande chose du monde, c'est de savoir être à soi); confirm placement in this essay.
Numbering follows the outline (1.39, Villey); Cotton numbers Of Solitude 1.38.
The parked-car and shop-curtain images are the writer's illustrations, not Montaigne's.
Refers back to day 1145 (the tower) by index; confirm against that script when written.
